title: The Water Cycle
description: REFERENCE: The Water Cycle. Water on Earth moves in a continuous loop. The Sun heats oceans, lakes, and rivers, and water evaporates into vapor. Plants release vapor too, a process called transpiration. Rising vapor cools and condenses into clouds. When droplets grow heavy, they fall as rain or snow — precipitation. Some water soaks into the ground (infiltration) and becomes groundwater; the rest flows over land as runoff back to rivers and oceans, and the cycle begins again. Nothing is created or destroyed; the same water dinosaurs drank still circulates today. Key facts: Evaporation turns liquid water into vapor. Transpiration is evaporation from plants. Condensation forms clouds. Precipitation returns water to the surface. About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water.

title: Photosynthesis
description: REFERENCE: Photosynthesis. Photosynthesis is how plants, algae, and some bacteria turn sunlight into food. Chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves, captures light energy. The organism takes in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil, then uses the light energy to assemble glucose — a sugar — releasing oxygen as a byproduct. In words: carbon dioxide plus water, with light, becomes glucose plus oxygen. Nearly all life depends on this process, directly or indirectly, for food and for the oxygen in the air. Key facts: Chlorophyll captures light energy. Inputs: carbon dioxide and water. Outputs: glucose and oxygen. It underpins most food chains.

title: The Solar System
description: REFERENCE: The Solar System. Our solar system is the Sun plus everything its gravity holds: eight planets, dwarf planets like Pluto, moons, asteroids, and comets. The four inner planets — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — are small and rocky. Beyond the asteroid belt, the four outer planets — Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune — are gas and ice giants. The Sun holds 99.8% of the system's mass. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth, and over 5 hours to reach Neptune. Key facts: Eight planets orbit the Sun. Inner planets are rocky; outer are giants. The Sun holds 99.8% of the system's mass. Sunlight takes ~8 minutes to reach Earth.

title: The Human Heart
description: REFERENCE: The Human Heart. The human heart is a muscular pump about the size of a fist. It has four chambers: two atria on top that receive blood, and two ventricles below that push it out. The right side collects oxygen-poor blood from the body and sends it to the lungs; the left side receives oxygen-rich blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body. One-way valves keep blood moving in the right direction. At rest it beats about 60-100 times per minute, moving roughly 7,500 liters of blood a day. Key facts: Four chambers: two atria, two ventricles. Right side serves the lungs; left serves the body. Valves enforce one-way flow. It pumps ~7,500 liters per day.

title: How the Internet Works
description: REFERENCE: How the Internet Works. The Internet is a global network of networks. Your device connects through an Internet service provider. Data is chopped into small packets, each labeled with its destination address (an IP address). Routers forward each packet hop by hop toward its destination, where packets are reassembled in order. Names like example.com are translated to IP addresses by the Domain Name System (DNS) — the Internet's phone book. No single machine runs the whole thing; it works because everyone follows the same protocols. Key facts: Data travels in packets. IP addresses identify destinations. DNS translates names to addresses. Routers forward packets hop by hop.

title: Democracy Basics
description: REFERENCE: Democracy Basics. Democracy is government by the people, usually through elected representatives. Its core features are free and fair elections, universal adult suffrage (the right to vote), rule of law that binds even leaders, protection of minority rights, and a free press. Citizens participate by voting, and in many systems also through petitions, juries, and public comment. Democracy's strength is peaceful transfer of power; its vulnerability is that it depends on an informed, participating public. Key facts: Power comes from voters through elections. Rule of law binds leaders too. Minority rights are protected. A free press enables informed voting.

title: The Scientific Method
description: REFERENCE: The Scientific Method. The scientific method is the loop by which science builds reliable knowledge: observe something, form a hypothesis (a testable explanation), predict what should happen if it's true, run an experiment or gather data, and analyze the results. If results contradict the hypothesis, revise it; if they support it, try harder tests. Findings are published so others can replicate them. A claim that survives repeated, independent testing becomes a theory — the strongest verdict in science. Key facts: Start with observation. Hypotheses must be testable. Experiments test predictions. Replication by others builds trust.

title: World War II Overview
description: REFERENCE: World War II Overview. World War II (1939-1945) was the largest conflict in history. It began when Germany invaded Poland in September 1939. The Axis powers — Germany, Italy, Japan — fought the Allies, led by Britain, the Soviet Union, and the United States. Key turning points included Stalingrad (1943), D-Day in Normandy (June 1944), and the Pacific island campaigns. The war ended in Europe in May 1945 and in the Pacific in August 1945. It caused tens of millions of deaths and led to the United Nations and the Cold War. Key facts: 1939-1945; began with the invasion of Poland. Axis vs. Allies. Turning points: Stalingrad, D-Day. Ended with the UN's founding era.

title: The Periodic Table
description: REFERENCE: The Periodic Table. The periodic table organizes all known chemical elements by atomic number — the count of protons. Dmitri Mendeleev's 1869 arrangement revealed the periodic law: elements in the same column share chemical behavior because they have the same number of outer electrons. Rows are periods; columns are groups. Metals sit left and center, nonmetals upper right, with metalloids along the boundary. The table even predicted elements before they were found — gallium and germanium were discovered because the table said to look. Key facts: Ordered by atomic number (proton count). Columns share chemical behavior. Mendeleev published it in 1869. It predicted undiscovered elements.

title: Gravity
description: REFERENCE: Gravity. Gravity is the attraction between masses. Newton described it as a force pulling masses together, proportional to their masses and weakening with distance squared — which explains falling apples and orbiting planets with one law. Einstein reframed it: mass curves spacetime, and objects follow the curves, which is why light itself bends near massive objects. On Earth, gravity accelerates falling objects at about 9.8 meters per second squared. It is the weakest fundamental force, yet it shapes stars, galaxies, and the universe's fate. Key facts: Newton: force between masses. Einstein: mass curves spacetime. Earth's surface gravity ~9.8 m/s^2. Weakest force, largest-scale effects.

title: The Brain
description: REFERENCE: The Brain. The human brain weighs about 1.4 kilograms and holds roughly 86 billion neurons. The cerebrum handles thought, memory, and voluntary movement; the cerebellum coordinates balance and fine motion; the brainstem runs breathing and heartbeat. Neurons communicate across synapses with electrical and chemical signals, and connections strengthen with use — the basis of learning. The brain uses about 20% of the body's energy despite being 2% of its weight. Key facts: ~86 billion neurons. Cerebrum: thought; cerebellum: coordination; brainstem: vital functions. Learning is strengthened synapses. Uses ~20% of the body's energy.

title: Electricity Basics
description: REFERENCE: Electricity Basics. Electricity is the flow of electric charge, usually electrons moving through a conductor. Voltage is the push (potential difference), current is the flow rate (amperes), and resistance opposes the flow (ohms) — related by Ohm's law: voltage equals current times resistance. Circuits need a complete loop to flow. Power, the rate of doing work, equals voltage times current and is measured in watts. Batteries store chemical energy as electricity; generators convert motion into it. Key facts: Current is flowing charge. Ohm's law: V = I x R. Power: P = V x I (watts). Circuits need a complete loop.

title: The Renaissance
description: REFERENCE: The Renaissance. The Renaissance ('rebirth') was the European cultural movement from roughly the 1300s to the 1600s that revived classical learning and launched modern art and science. Centered first in Italian city-states, it produced Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael in art; Petrarch and Erasmus in letters; and the printing press (c. 1440), which spread ideas faster than ever. Humanism — the study of human potential — reshaped education, and the era's curiosity fed directly into the Scientific Revolution. Key facts: ~1300s-1600s, centered first in Italy. Revived classical art and learning. The printing press spread ideas. Fed into the Scientific Revolution.

title: Climate and Weather
description: REFERENCE: Climate and Weather. Weather is the atmosphere's state right now — temperature, rain, wind, humidity. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather in a region, typically averaged over 30 years. Both are driven by the Sun heating Earth unevenly: hot air rises at the equator and sinks elsewhere, creating wind belts, while ocean currents move heat around the planet. Greenhouse gases trap outgoing heat; without them Earth would be frozen, but adding more warms the climate. Deserts, rainforests, and tundra are climate zones shaped by these flows. Key facts: Weather is short-term; climate is the 30-year pattern. Uneven solar heating drives winds. Oceans move heat globally. Greenhouse gases trap heat.

title: The Stock Market
description: REFERENCE: The Stock Market. A stock is a slice of ownership in a company. The stock market is where those slices are bought and sold, through exchanges like the NYSE. Prices move with supply and demand, driven by company earnings, economic news, and investor expectations. An index like the S&P 500 tracks a basket of stocks as a market summary. Over long periods, diversified stock holdings have historically grown, but prices swing — risk and return travel together. (General information, not financial advice.) Key facts: A stock is part-ownership of a company. Prices follow supply and demand. Indexes summarize baskets of stocks. Risk and return travel together.

title: Human Rights
description: REFERENCE: Human Rights. Human rights are basic protections owed to every person. The 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights lists them: life, liberty, equality before the law, free speech, freedom of belief, education, and more. They bind governments, not just individuals — the point is that state power has limits. Rights are enforced through national constitutions and courts, plus international treaties and tribunals. They are called universal because they don't depend on citizenship. Key facts: The UDHR was adopted in 1948. Rights limit government power. They apply regardless of citizenship. Enforced via courts and treaties.

title: The Theory of Evolution
description: REFERENCE: The Theory of Evolution. Evolution by natural selection, published by Charles Darwin in 1859, explains life's diversity: organisms vary, more offspring are born than survive, and the variants best suited to the environment tend to reproduce — so useful traits spread over generations. Given enough time, this process produces new species. The evidence spans fossils showing transitions, DNA revealing shared ancestry, observed selection (like antibiotic resistance), and experiments. It is one of science's best-supported theories. (Evidence status: strong, multi-line evidence.) Key facts: Published by Darwin in 1859. Mechanism: variation + selection over time. Evidence: fossils, DNA, observed selection. Status: strong multi-line evidence.

title: The Printing Press
description: REFERENCE: The Printing Press. Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type printing press (c. 1440) made books cheap for the first time. Before it, books were copied by hand and cost a fortune; after it, a single press could print thousands of copies. Literacy spread, scientists shared results, reformers spread ideas, and newspapers eventually followed. Historians rank it among the most consequential inventions ever — it industrialized the spread of knowledge itself. Key facts: Gutenberg, c. 1440. Movable type made books cheap. Spread literacy and science. Enabled newspapers and mass media.

title: Antibiotics
description: REFERENCE: Antibiotics. Antibiotics are drugs that kill or stop bacteria. Alexander Fleming noticed penicillin mold killing bacteria in 1928; Florey and Chain turned it into a medicine in the 1940s, saving countless lives in WWII and after. They work by attacking bacterial machinery — cell walls, protein-building — that human cells don't share. They do nothing against viruses. Overuse breeds resistant bacteria, which is why doctors stress finishing prescriptions and not demanding antibiotics for colds. Key facts: Penicillin: Fleming 1928; medicine in the 1940s. Target bacteria-specific machinery. Useless against viruses. Overuse breeds resistance.

title: The United Nations
description: REFERENCE: The United Nations. The United Nations, founded in 1945 after World War II, is the main forum where the world's countries talk instead of fight. Its jobs include keeping peace (peacekeeping missions), delivering humanitarian aid, setting international law, and coordinating on health and development. The Security Council handles crises; the General Assembly gives every member state a voice. It has real limits — great powers can veto action — but it remains the closest thing to a world parliament. Key facts: Founded 1945. Peacekeeping, aid, international law. Security Council handles crises. Every member state gets a General Assembly voice.
